courses.title: How neurotoxins work
courses.summary: What botulinum toxin type A is, how it quiets a muscle, and why the effect is temporary.

lessons.title: From nerve signal to softer line
body: Every expression line starts with a muscle. When you frown, a nerve releases a chemical messenger called acetylcholine at the spot where it meets the muscle, and the muscle contracts. Repeat that thousands of times and the skin above it creases.

Botulinum toxin type A is a purified protein made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum. Once injected into a muscle, it is taken up by the nerve endings and cuts a protein called SNAP-25 that the nerve needs to release acetylcholine. No release means no signal, so that part of the muscle relaxes (Pirazzini et al., 2017).

The nerve is not destroyed. Over the following weeks it sprouts new connections and the original junction recovers, which is why the effect fades and movement returns. For facial lines, the FDA labels and most clinic sources describe about 3 to 4 months of effect (Botox Cosmetic label; AAD).

Because the toxin works on the muscle, it softens dynamic lines, the ones you see when you move. Lines etched into the skin at rest improve more slowly and sometimes need other treatments such as resurfacing or filler (Small, American Family Physician, 2026).

body.text: The same molecule causes botulism when it enters the body in large, uncontrolled amounts. Medical products are measured in tiny, standardized units, made under FDA manufacturing controls, and placed into specific muscles. That control is what separates a treatment from a poisoning (Mayo Clinic).

lessons.title: Cosmetic and medical uses
body: Botulinum toxin was a medical drug before it was a cosmetic one. OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) is FDA approved for conditions including chronic migraine, cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, overactive bladder and severe underarm sweating, under a separate label from Botox Cosmetic (Botox label).

The first cosmetic approval came in 2002 for glabellar lines, the 11s between the brows. Botox Cosmetic has since added crow's feet, forehead lines and, in October 2024, platysma bands of the neck (Botox Cosmetic label).

Many popular treatments, such as the lip flip, masseter slimming, gummy smile and chin treatments, are off-label. Off-label means a licensed prescriber uses an approved drug for a purpose or site that is not on the label. It is legal and common, but the doses come from studies and expert consensus rather than FDA review, so ranges vary more between injectors (Sundaram et al., 2016).

Knowing whether a treatment is on-label helps you ask better questions. For a labeled area you can read the exact studied dose. For an off-label area, ask your injector what dose range they use and why.

lessons.title: The six FDA-approved cosmetic toxins
body: As of this writing there are six botulinum toxin type A products with FDA approval for cosmetic use in the United States. All six carry the same boxed warning about distant spread of toxin effect.

items: Botox Cosmetic (onabotulinumtoxinA, AbbVie): glabellar, crow's feet, forehead and platysma bands.
Dysport (abobotulinumtoxinA, Galderma): glabellar lines. May contain trace cow's milk protein, which is a listed contraindication for people with that allergy.
Xeomin (incobotulinumtoxinA, Merz): upper facial lines, meaning glabellar, forehead and crow's feet, up to 64 units when all three are treated.
Jeuveau (prabotulinumtoxinA-xvfs, Evolus): glabellar lines.
Daxxify (daxibotulinumtoxinA-lanm, Revance): glabellar lines. Formulated with a 35 amino acid stabilizing peptide (RTP004); its listed ingredients include no human albumin.
Letybo (letibotulinumtoxinA-wlbg, Hugel): glabellar lines, approved February 29, 2024.

body: Every one of these labels says the same thing about retreatment: no more often than every 3 months (each product's label).

Products sold abroad, such as Nabota, Meditoxin, Innotox, Coretox or Hutox, are not FDA approved for use in the U.S. even when a related product is. A vial imported outside the authorized supply chain is unapproved in the U.S. regardless of how it is labeled, which is one reason the FDA and CDC warn against buying toxin online (FDA; CDC MMWR 2025).

body.text: Your tracker lets you log Korean and other non-U.S. products because some people are treated abroad. Logging is not an endorsement. If you were treated outside the U.S., keep the product name, lot number and clinic details in case you ever need them.

lessons.title: Why units are not interchangeable
body: A unit of botulinum toxin is a measure of biological activity, not weight. Each company measures its own product with its own assay, so the labels state plainly that units of one product cannot be compared to or converted into units of another (Botox Cosmetic, Xeomin and Jeuveau labels).

That is why the glabellar dose looks so different on paper: 20 units of Botox Cosmetic, Xeomin, Jeuveau or Letybo, 50 units of Dysport, and 40 units of Daxxify. The patient is not getting more toxin with Dysport; the unit is simply a different size.

In practice, clinicians use working ratios. Incobotulinum (Xeomin) has performed like onabotulinum (Botox) at about 1 to 1. For abobotulinum (Dysport), a review by Scaglione (2016) suggests about 3 Dysport units to 1 Botox unit or lower for medical uses, and aesthetic practice often uses about 2.5 to 1. These are rules of thumb, not label instructions.

When you log a treatment, record the product name and the units exactly as your injector told you. The app's Botox-equivalent total is an approximation for comparing your own history over time, not a dosing tool.

body.text: Never use a conversion ratio to plan a dose. Dosing decisions belong to the licensed injector who examined you.

courses.title: Facial anatomy for neurotoxin treatment
courses.summary: The muscles injectors treat, the ones they protect, and the danger zones on your face map.

lessons.title: Elevators, depressors and balance
body: The face works in opposing pairs. In the upper face, the frontalis is the only muscle that lifts the brows. Pulling the other way are the brow depressors: the corrugators and procerus between the brows and the outer orbicularis oculi around the eye.

Neurotoxin treatment is mostly about shifting that balance. Relax the depressors and the brow can rise slightly. Relax too much of the frontalis and the brow can drop. This push and pull explains why forehead and frown lines are planned together (Botox Cosmetic label).

In the lower face the same logic applies. The depressor anguli oris pulls the mouth corners down, while the zygomaticus major and minor lift the smile. The mentalis pushes the chin up and puckers it. The platysma, a thin sheet in the neck, pulls the jawline and lower face down.

On your face map, muscles you can tap for treatment are drawn with the concern they are known for. Muscles like the zygomaticus, risorius and the upper eyelid's levator are shown as caution zones: injectors work to keep toxin away from them.

items: Upper face: frontalis (lifts), corrugator and procerus (pull down and in), orbicularis oculi (closes and squints).
Mid face: nasalis (bunny lines), levator labii superioris alaeque nasi (lifts the lip and nostril).
Lower face: orbicularis oris (purses the lips), depressor anguli oris (pulls corners down), mentalis (chin), masseter (chewing).
Neck: platysma (vertical bands, jawline pull).

lessons.title: Danger zones and safe distances
body: Most toxin side effects are predictable from anatomy. The toxin spreads a short distance from where it is placed, so injectors keep set distances from structures they want to protect.

items: Upper eyelid: the levator palpebrae superioris lifts the lid. The Botox Cosmetic label tells injectors to place lateral corrugator injections at least 1 cm above the bony brow ridge to reduce eyelid ptosis.
Brow: frontalis points are kept well above the brow, often about 1.5 to 2 cm in consensus papers, so the brow keeps its lift.
Eye corner: the first crow's feet point on the label sits about 1.5 to 2 cm outside the eye corner and just outside the bony orbital rim, with the needle angled away from the eye.
Smile: points around the cheek and mouth stay off the diagonal line of the zygomaticus.
Lower lip: chin and mouth-corner points stay away from the depressor labii inferioris so the lower lip still moves normally.
Neck: platysma points are kept superficial, because deeper neck muscles control swallowing and voice.

body: Researchers have also found anatomical shortcuts. A 2021 review describes a supraorbital foramen in some people that can act as a pathway from the brow area toward the muscle that lifts the eyelid (Nestor et al., 2021). That is one reason experienced injectors map each face rather than using one template.

body.text: The app's caution zones are educational markers drawn from the label and consensus papers. They are not a guide for placing injections.

lessons.title: Who can legally inject
body: In every U.S. state, injecting a prescription neurotoxin is treated as the practice of medicine. The details differ by state, but the pattern is consistent (American Med Spa Association; AAFE).

items: Physicians (MD or DO) can evaluate, prescribe and inject.
Nurse practitioners can inject within their state's scope; some states require a collaborative agreement with a physician.
Physician assistants inject under physician supervision or collaboration.
Registered nurses usually inject under a physician's or NP's order and supervision, after a patient exam.
Dentists may inject in many states, often limited to the mouth and face area of their practice.
Estheticians, cosmetologists and unlicensed people cannot inject toxin. A weekend course does not change that.

body: Certification is not a license. A training certificate shows someone took a course. The license, held by a state board, is what makes injecting legal. The AAFE, a training provider, describes certification as the step after licensure, never a substitute for it.

Toxin is a prescription drug, so a licensed prescriber must evaluate you, often in person, before it is given. Supervision rules for nurses vary: some states require the physician on site, others allow phone availability. Your state's medical and nursing boards publish the rules.

body.text: For licensed clinicians who want hands-on skills: accredited CME courses from groups such as the American Academy of Facial Esthetics, National Laser Institute and Empire Medical Training, plus manufacturer programs such as the Allergan Medical Institute, teach supervised technique on live models. Check your own state board for what your license allows before enrolling.

lessons.title: Vetting an injector and a clinic
body: Skill matters more than the brand of toxin. The American Board of Cosmetic Surgery calls the injector's expertise the single most important factor in a safe, natural result, and the AAD recommends treatment by a board-certified dermatologist or a member of that doctor's staff.

Board certification is a separate step beyond a license. An ABMS member board, such as the American Board of Dermatology or American Board of Plastic Surgery, certifies that a physician passed an independent evaluation in a specialty. You can check certification through the boards' own lookup tools.

items: Who will inject me, and what is their license?
How many of this exact treatment do you do each month?
Which product will you use, how many units, and can I see the vial?
Do you buy directly from the manufacturer or an authorized distributor?
Who do I call if something seems wrong, and do you see patients for a 2-week follow-up?
Can I see before and after photos of your own patients?

body: Red flags include prices far below market, injections at parties or in homes, reluctance to show the vial, no medical history taken, and pressure to treat more areas than you asked about (ABCS; AmSpa; CDC).

A good consultation includes a medical history, a look at how your face moves, a discussion of risks, and a plan that matches what you want. The provider should be glad to answer questions before anything is drawn up.

lessons.title: What happens at the appointment
body: Before treatment, tell your injector about your medications, supplements, any neuromuscular condition, allergies, recent illness, and whether you are pregnant, breastfeeding or planning a pregnancy (AAD Preparation). Blood thinners and some supplements can raise the chance of bruising, but do not stop a prescribed medicine without talking to the doctor who prescribed it.

A typical visit takes 10 to 30 minutes. The injector watches you frown, raise your brows and smile to see which muscles are strongest, may mark points, cleans the skin, and uses a very fine needle to place small amounts into each muscle. Several areas can be treated in one visit (Cleveland Clinic).
Ask what product and how many units were used in each area, and write it down or log it in the app right away. That record is what lets your injector adjust next time.
Taking standardized photos before treatment, at rest and with each expression, makes the day 14 check far more useful. The app's check-in feature is built for this.

lessons.title: Aftercare and the results timeline
body: Common aftercare advice includes not rubbing or massaging the treated area, waiting before strenuous exercise, and not pressing makeup in. The AAD says to avoid rubbing and to wait 2 hours before strenuous activity; many clinics add staying upright for about 4 hours.

How much of this is proven? A 2025 study of about 5,000 upper-face patients who followed only a 10-minute precaution protocol found no eyelid ptosis and high satisfaction, but it had no control group (Santorelli et al., 2025). The fair summary is that most aftercare rules are reasonable caution with limited evidence; technique and dose matter more.

items: Day 0 to 1: small bumps fade within an hour; redness or tenderness for a few hours.
Days 2 to 4: most people notice the first change; Daxxify and Dysport are often described as a little faster.
Days 10 to 14: full effect. The Xeomin label gives a median onset of 2 to 7 days, and Cleveland Clinic and the American Family Physician review put full results at about 2 weeks.
Weeks 1 to 2: bruises, if any, usually clear within about a week (AAD).
Months 3 to 4: movement returns for most products; Daxxify averages longer, about 24 weeks in trials (ASPS).

body: Wait the full 2 weeks before judging the result or asking for a touch-up. Effects build gradually, and one side can settle a few days later than the other.

body.text: Trouble swallowing, speaking or breathing after any toxin treatment is a medical emergency. Call 911 or go to the emergency room. The Safety courses cover this in detail.

lessons.title: Touch-ups and the 2-week check
body: The 2-week visit is where fine-tuning happens. By then the toxin has reached its full effect, so the injector can see what is still moving and whether both sides match.

A touch-up is a small additional dose to even out asymmetry or catch a strong area that was missed, such as a lateral brow that lifts too much. It is a judgment call: adding toxin to an area that is still settling can overshoot.

Some side effects are not fixable with more toxin. A heavy or dropped brow, for example, usually has to wait for the forehead to recover, though a skilled injector may sometimes rebalance nearby muscles (Kassir et al., 2020).
Record touch-ups as their own entry with the date, product and units. In the app, that keeps your totals and day counts accurate.

lessons.title: Planning intervals and long-term use
body: Every FDA cosmetic toxin label says retreatment should be no more frequent than every 3 months. Most people return when movement comes back, often at 3 to 4 months; Daxxify users often wait longer.

Why not sooner? Frequent dosing and high cumulative doses are thought to raise the small risk of developing neutralizing antibodies, which can make future treatments work less well. Rates in modern trials are very low. In pooled Daxxify trials, no subject developed neutralizing antibodies (Gallagher et al., 2023).

The labels also tell clinicians to consider the cumulative dose when a person receives toxin for more than one reason, for example cosmetic treatment plus migraine treatment. If you get toxin from more than one provider, tell each of them.
With regular treatment some people find results last a little longer over time, which the AAD attributes to the muscle thinning with repeated use.

courses.title: Forehead lines
courses.summary: Horizontal lines from the frontalis, the label pattern, and how injectors avoid a heavy brow.

lessons.title: The frontalis and the labeled pattern
body: Horizontal forehead lines come from the frontalis, a thin vertical sheet of muscle that runs from the hairline to the brow skin. It is the only muscle that lifts the eyebrows, so every unit placed there is a trade between smoother skin and brow height.

Forehead lines became the third Botox Cosmetic indication, after frown lines and crow's feet (PRS Global Open review, 2020). The label calls for 4 units into each of 5 forehead sites (20 units) together with 20 units in the glabellar complex, 40 units total, because treating the frontalis alone makes brow drop more likely. Xeomin's upper facial lines label uses the same 20 plus 20 structure.

The label tells injectors to find the treatment rows by feeling the forehead at rest and at full brow raise, and to consider the size of the forehead and where the muscle is most active. Consensus papers describe keeping forehead points well above the brow, commonly about 1.5 to 2 cm (Sundaram et al., 2016).
In the forehead trials, headache (9 percent) and brow ptosis (2 percent) were the most common adverse reactions, along with eyelid ptosis and a sense of skin tightness (Botox Cosmetic label).

lessons.title: Heavy brows, Spock brows and individual foreheads
body: Two problems dominate forehead treatment. A heavy or dropped brow happens when too much of the lower frontalis is relaxed, especially in people who already use their forehead to hold their brows up. A Spock or Mephisto brow is the opposite: the center is relaxed while the outer frontalis still pulls, so the brow tails arch upward.

A heavy brow usually has to wait out the toxin. A Spock brow can often be softened at the 2-week visit with a very small dose in the overactive outer fibers, which is one reason the follow-up visit matters.

People with low-set brows, hooded upper lids or lids that already sag often rely on the frontalis to see clearly. A careful injector will notice that you raise your brows at rest and treat higher, lighter or not at all. Some people are better served by an eyelid or brow evaluation than by more toxin.

Forehead height matters too. A tall forehead may get a second row of points; a short one may get fewer, smaller doses. The label itself tells injectors to account for forehead size and the distribution of muscle activity.

lessons.title: The frown complex and the five-point pattern
body: The 11s are vertical lines between the brows made mainly by the paired corrugator supercilii, which pull the brows down and together, and the procerus, which pulls the space between the brows down and creates a horizontal line at the bridge of the nose.

This is the most studied cosmetic toxin site. All six FDA-approved cosmetic products are labeled for it, and their labels use the same five-site layout: one point in the procerus and two in each corrugator.

items: Botox Cosmetic, Xeomin, Jeuveau and Letybo: 4 units per site, 20 units total.
Dysport: 10 units per site, 50 units total.
Daxxify: 8 units per site, 40 units total.

body: Doses are individualized. Consensus papers note that people with stronger muscles, which often includes men, may need more than the labeled starting dose, while a three-point version is sometimes used for lighter frowns (Carruthers et al., 2004; Sundaram et al., 2016).

lessons.title: Why eyelid droop is the glabellar risk
body: The muscle that lifts the upper eyelid, the levator palpebrae superioris, sits just below the brow behind the orbital rim. Toxin that drifts there causes eyelid ptosis: one lid sits lower and can feel heavy.
In the Botox Cosmetic glabellar trials, eyelid ptosis was the most common adverse reaction at 3 percent. It was 2 percent in the Daxxify and Jeuveau programs (each product's label).

The labels list concrete steps to reduce it: avoid injecting near the levator, especially in people with larger brow depressors; keep lateral corrugator injections at least 1 cm above the bony ridge; keep volume and dose accurate and as low as feasible; and do not inject closer than 1 cm above the central eyebrow.

Ptosis from toxin typically appears 3 to 14 days after treatment and resolves on its own as the toxin wears off. A physician may prescribe eye drops that can partly lift the lid in the meantime (Nestor et al., 2021). The Safety courses explain what to do if it happens.

body.text: If both eyelids droop, or a droopy lid comes with double vision, slurred speech or trouble swallowing, that is not a typical local side effect. Seek urgent care.

lessons.title: The orbicularis oculi and the labeled pattern
body: Crow's feet are the lines that fan out from the outer corner of the eye when you smile or squint. They come from the outer part of the orbicularis oculi, a ring of muscle that closes the eye.
Botox Cosmetic is labeled for crow's feet, and Xeomin is labeled for them as part of upper facial lines. Both use 4 units in each of 3 sites per side, 24 units total.

The Botox Cosmetic label places the first point about 1.5 to 2.0 cm toward the temple from the outer eye corner and just outside the bony orbital rim, with the other points above and below it depending on where the lines are. It directs the needle bevel up and pointed away from the eye.

Eyelid edema (1 percent) was the most common adverse reaction in the crow's feet trials. Points placed too low risk reaching the zygomaticus, which lifts the smile, so an injector watches your smile before choosing points.

courses.title: Brow lift
courses.summary: How relaxing brow depressors can raise the brow tail, and who it suits.

lessons.title: Lifting by relaxing the depressors
body: A toxin brow lift does not add lift. It removes some of the downward pull so the frontalis, which still works, can raise the brow a little more. The usual target is the outer orbicularis oculi under the brow tail, and sometimes the frown muscles between the brows.

Ahn and colleagues described a temporal brow lift with toxin in 2000, reporting a measurable rise of the lateral brow after treating the upper outer orbicularis oculi (Ahn et al., 2000). Results are typically a few millimeters, not a surgical lift.

This is off-label. Doses in expert practice are small, often a few units per side, and the placement has to respect the frontalis above it. If the outer forehead is also treated heavily, the tail can drop instead of rise.

It suits people with mild tail droop and a healthy frontalis. It does not fix excess eyelid skin or significant brow ptosis, and a heavy hand can produce a surprised or Spock look. An oculoplastic or facial plastic evaluation is the next step when the issue is lid skin rather than brow position.

courses.summary: Diagonal lines on the nose, the newest anatomy research, and protecting the upper lip.

lessons.title: The nasalis and the bunny triangle
body: Bunny lines are the diagonal wrinkles on the sides of the upper nose when you scrunch. They are traditionally blamed on the nasalis muscle and often become more noticeable once the frown lines are treated.

A 2025 cadaver and ultrasound study found a muscle-free area beneath the lines, which the authors called the bunny triangle, bordered by the procerus, nasalis, orbicularis oculi and the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi (LLSAN). They concluded that injecting straight into the wrinkles may hit connective tissue instead of muscle, and that targeting the muscle borders may work better (Ahn et al., 2025).

The main risk is spread to the LLSAN or nearby lip elevators, which can make the upper lip feel heavy or change the smile. An aesthetics educator's short video below walks through these side effects. Doses in practice are small and off-label.
Toxin around the nose is also marketed for reshaping the nasal tip. A board-certified dermatologist's review of that trend is a useful reality check on what toxin can and cannot change.

lessons.title: The lip flip
body: A lip flip places a very small amount of toxin in the orbicularis oris along the upper lip border. Relaxing that edge lets the lip roll outward slightly, so more of the pink shows when you smile. It adds no volume, which is the key difference from filler.

A 2025 systematic review found seven studies that reported sites and doses. The procedure typically used 4 to 6 units in the orbicularis oris, with high satisfaction and mild, temporary side effects such as trouble whistling or drinking through a straw (Pitchford et al., 2025).

Cleveland Clinic describes about 2 to 4 units in the upper lip and about 2 in the lower lip, results within about a week, and an effect lasting 2 to 5 months, shorter than many other areas because the lips move constantly.

Vertical lip lines, often called smoker's lines, can also be softened with small doses in the same muscle, but etched lines usually need resurfacing or filler as well. Too much toxin here can cause drooling, trouble with straws, or changes in speech until it wears off.

lessons.title: Treating a gummy smile
body: A gummy smile shows more gum than a person likes when they smile fully. One cause is an overactive group of upper lip elevators: the levator labii superioris, the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi (LLSAN) beside the nose, and the zygomaticus minor.

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis found that toxin in these muscles, at doses from about 1.25 to 7.5 units per side, reduced gum display. Compared with controls, the mean reduction was about 2.5 mm at 2 weeks and about 2.2 mm at 3 months, with results fading gradually (Rojo-Sanchis et al., 2023).

Toxin only helps when the cause is muscular. A gummy smile from excess vertical growth of the upper jaw, gums that cover too much of the teeth, or other dental causes needs a dental, orthodontic or surgical evaluation. The same review excluded those causes from its analysis.
Too much effect can lengthen the upper lip, flatten the smile or make it uneven, which is why doses are small and the zygomaticus major is avoided.

lessons.title: Relaxing the depressor anguli oris
body: The depressor anguli oris (DAO) is a small triangular muscle that runs from the jawbone up to the corner of the mouth. When it is strong, it pulls the corners down, which can give a sad or tired look and deepen marionette lines.

A 2026 Italian consensus that also reviewed 16 international consensus papers found that both groups used a mean total of about 5.6 units for the DAO. Nearly all of the 14 experts preferred an intramuscular injection at a single point lateral to the marionette line, staying in a safe zone away from the depressor labii inferioris (Fundaro et al., 2026).

The danger is spread to the depressor labii inferioris, which moves the lower lip, or to the risorius and zygomaticus, which shape the smile. That can cause an uneven lower lip, a crooked smile or drooling until it wears off. Sources differ on the exact safe distance from the mouth corner, so placement is very injector-dependent.
Toxin softens the pull; it does not replace lost volume. Deep marionette lines from volume loss often need filler or other treatments in addition.

lessons.title: Relaxing the mentalis
body: The mentalis is a paired cone-shaped muscle at the tip of the chin. It lifts and puckers the chin skin and pushes the lower lip up. When it is overactive the chin gets a dimpled, golf ball or orange peel texture, and the crease under the lower lip can deepen.

The 2026 Italian consensus listed orange peel chin and mentalis hyperactivity as the main indications. The Italian panel recommended a mean total of 8 units split between both sides, slightly higher than the 6.5 unit international average, often combining injections into the muscle and into the skin (Fundaro et al., 2026).
Points are placed low on the chin near the midline. Toxin that spreads upward or outward can weaken the lower lip, making it harder to close the lips, causing drooling, or making the smile uneven.

Chin dimpling sometimes reflects a short or retruded chin that the mentalis is straining to support. In that case an injector may discuss filler or a surgical opinion along with, or instead of, toxin.

lessons.title: Masseter treatment for jaw width
body: The masseter is a thick chewing muscle at the angle of the jaw. When it is large, from genetics or from clenching, it widens the lower face. Toxin relaxes the muscle and, over weeks, it shrinks, which can narrow the jawline.

A 2026 meta-analysis pooled five randomized, placebo-controlled trials with 536 participants. Toxin improved masseter prominence scores, reduced muscle thickness and raised satisfaction; trial regimens of 48 and 72 units total both showed benefit. The authors found too much variation to define an optimal dose or protocol (Machado et al., 2026).
This is off-label in the U.S. Slimming takes longer than wrinkle treatment because the change comes from the muscle shrinking, so it is judged over several weeks rather than at day 14.

Injectors keep points in the lower, back part of the muscle, away from the front edge where the risorius and smile muscles sit. Possible side effects include chewing fatigue, a changed smile if toxin spreads forward, and a bulge if part of the muscle is missed.

lessons.title: Clenching, grinding and TMJ pain
body: Many people ask for masseter treatment because they clench or grind their teeth (bruxism) or have jaw pain. The evidence here is more mixed than for jaw slimming.

A 2022 systematic review of 24 randomized trials concluded there is good evidence for toxin in masseter hypertrophy, equivocal evidence for muscle-related jaw pain disorders, and very little evidence for disorders of the jaw joint itself. Doses and methods varied widely (Delcanho et al., 2022).

Jaw pain has many causes. A dentist or physician who treats temporomandibular disorders should evaluate pain, clicking, locking or headaches before toxin is chosen, and a night guard or other treatment may be part of the plan.
Because the masseter is a chewing muscle, people sometimes notice tired chewing with tough foods in the first weeks. That usually settles as the effect plateaus.

lessons.title: The temporalis, migraine and tension
body: The temporalis is a fan-shaped chewing muscle over the temple. It works with the masseter to close the jaw, and people who clench often feel it tighten.

The temporalis is part of the FDA-labeled chronic migraine protocol for Botox, the therapeutic product. The label calls for 155 units across seven head and neck muscle areas every 12 weeks, including 40 units in 8 temporalis sites (Botox label). That is a medical treatment for chronic migraine, prescribed after a headache evaluation, not a cosmetic one.
For tension-type headache and clenching-related temple pain, the evidence is weaker and treatment is off-label. Reviews of toxin for jaw-muscle pain report mixed results (Delcanho et al., 2022).
Temple treatment for cosmetic reasons is uncommon. Weakening the temporalis can make the temple look more hollow in some people, so this area is usually approached for function, not appearance.

body.text: If you have frequent headaches, start with a physician who treats headache. Chronic migraine has its own diagnosis and its own labeled dose, very different from cosmetic treatment.

lessons.title: Platysma bands and the 2024 label
body: The platysma is a thin sheet of muscle that runs from the upper chest over the neck and into the lower face. With age its edges can stand out as vertical bands, and its pull can blur the jawline.

In October 2024 the FDA added moderate to severe platysma bands to the Botox Cosmetic label. The labeled pattern uses 2 units at each of 4 sites in the upper platysma just below the jawline on each side, plus 1 unit at each of 5 sites along each treated vertical band, with 1 to 2 bands per side.

items: One band per side: 26 units in 18 sites.
One band on one side, two on the other: 31 units in 23 sites.
Two bands per side: 36 units in 28 sites.

body: In a sponsor-funded phase 3 repeat-treatment study, 83.6 percent of participants improved by at least one grade after the first cycle, rising to 98 percent by the fourth. Treatment-related events were mild, though a few participants reported events of special interest such as difficulty swallowing (Mraz et al., 2026).

lessons.title: Jawline contouring and neck risks
body: Before the label existed, injectors treated the platysma along the jawline to sharpen it, a technique Levy described in 2007 as the Nefertiti lift. The idea is to reduce the platysma's downward pull on the lower face (Levy, 2007). The label's jawline sites follow a similar logic.

Results are modest. Toxin can soften bands and slightly improve definition, but it does not remove loose skin or fat. People with significant laxity are often better candidates for surgical options, which a plastic or facial plastic surgeon can discuss.

The neck is where distant spread matters most. Deeper neck muscles help with swallowing, voice and holding the head up. Labels and reviews warn about difficulty swallowing, voice changes and neck weakness, so injections are kept superficial and doses controlled.

body.text: New trouble swallowing, a hoarse or weak voice, or difficulty holding up your head after neck treatment needs prompt medical care. Trouble breathing is an emergency: call 911.

lessons.title: Common and expected reactions
body: Most side effects are mild, local and short-lived, and come from the needle more than the toxin (AAD). Expect some of these in the first hours or days.

items: Small bumps at the injection points that settle within about an hour.
Redness, tenderness or mild swelling for a few hours.
Bruising, which the AAD says lasts about a week.

Headache in the first days. It was the most common reaction in several trials: 9 percent in the Botox Cosmetic forehead studies, 12 percent with Jeuveau, 6 percent with Daxxify and 2 percent with Letybo (each product's label).
Eyelid swelling after crow's feet treatment, about 1 percent in the Botox Cosmetic trials.
Dry eye. The Botox Cosmetic label tells patients to report eye dryness, pain, irritation, light sensitivity or vision changes.

body: A 2016 meta-analysis of 16 placebo-controlled facial trials found that frown-line treatment carried significantly more headache and eyelid ptosis than placebo, while crow's feet treatment showed no significant increase except bruising at the injection site (Jia et al., 2016).
Comparing rates across products is tricky. Each label notes that trials were run under different conditions, so a lower number on one label does not prove that product is safer.

lessons.title: Ptosis, asymmetry and other complications
body: Brow ptosis and asymmetry are the most common true complications of toxin, according to a narrative review (Kassir et al., 2020). Most come from toxin acting on a muscle next to the one that was targeted.

items: Eyelid ptosis: one upper lid sits lower, usually 3 to 14 days after frown or brow treatment. It resolves as the toxin wears off. A physician may prescribe eye drops, such as apraclonidine or oxymetazoline, that partly lift the lid in the meantime (Nestor et al., 2021).
Brow ptosis or a heavy forehead: the brow drops after forehead treatment. It generally waits out the toxin.
Spock brow: an arched brow tail when the outer forehead is still active. Often adjustable at the 2-week visit.
Smile changes: a crooked smile, uneven lower lip or drooling after mouth, chin, cheek or masseter treatment.
Lip function: trouble with straws, whistling or certain sounds after a lip flip.
Chewing fatigue after masseter treatment.
Swallowing or voice changes after neck treatment. These need prompt medical review.

body: The key way to tell a local side effect from something more serious is pattern. A one-sided droop near the treated area is typical of local spread. Weakness on both sides, double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing or breathing, or weakness in the arms points to a wider effect and is urgent (CDC).
Call your injector for any new droop or asymmetry. Photos with the date help, and the app's check-ins make this easy. Report significant reactions to FDA MedWatch as well.

body.text: Trouble breathing, swallowing or speaking after a toxin injection is an emergency. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room now. Do not wait for a callback from the clinic.

lessons.title: The boxed warning and when to get help
body: Every botulinum toxin product carries the FDA's strongest warning, a boxed warning titled Distant Spread of Toxin Effect. It says the effects may spread beyond the injection area and cause generalized weakness, double vision, drooping eyelids, trouble swallowing, hoarse voice, slurred speech, loss of bladder control and breathing difficulty, from hours to weeks after injection. Swallowing and breathing problems can be life threatening, and deaths have been reported (Botox Cosmetic label).

Context matters. The label states that no definitive serious reports of distant spread have been tied to dermatologic use of Botox Cosmetic at its labeled cosmetic doses. Most serious cases involve large medical doses, people with underlying neuromuscular conditions, or counterfeit and mishandled product (Botox Cosmetic label; CDC HAN 00507).

items: Call 911 or go to an emergency room now for: trouble breathing, trouble swallowing or choking on liquids, inability to hold up your head, or weakness spreading to the arms or body.
Seek same-day urgent care for: double or blurred vision, drooping of both eyelids, slurred speech, a new hoarse voice, or dry mouth with weakness.
Call your injector within a day or two for: a droop or asymmetry limited to the treated area, a heavy brow, or a smile change.

body: Tell the emergency team what product you received, the date, the areas, the units, and where it came from. If counterfeit or unapproved product is suspected, they can contact the health department and the CDC's botulism service, which provides antitoxin when botulism is suspected (CDC).

lessons.title: What happened in 2024 and 2025
body: In April 2024 the FDA warned that counterfeit Botox had been found in multiple states and injected for cosmetic purposes. Reported effects included blurred or double vision, trouble swallowing, dry mouth, shortness of breath and weakness. The injections were given by licensed and unlicensed people, often in nonmedical settings, using product bought from unlicensed sources (FDA).

The CDC's April 2024 health advisory counted 22 people in 11 jurisdictions. All were women aged 25 to 59, 11 of 20 with information were hospitalized, and 6 received botulism antitoxin. All had been injected by unlicensed or untrained people or in nonmedical settings such as homes or spas (CDC HAN 00507).

A CDC report on seven of those patients found injections in homes and a spa, a product carton claiming 150 units with a batch number from a legitimate vial that expired in 2017, and one patient who paid less than the U.S. wholesale price (MMWR, July 2024).

In 2025, three women in New York, Texas and Wisconsin injected themselves with toxin bought online from overseas vendors contacted through messaging apps and social media. All were hospitalized, one needed a ventilator, and all received antitoxin (MMWR, 2025). The CDC later reported 13 severely ill patients over 10 months from do-it-yourself injection, many using unlabeled vials of white powder (CDC, 2026).

body.text: Never buy botulinum toxin online and never inject yourself. The CDC says people without a health care license should not buy it, and products from unlicensed sources may be counterfeit, contaminated, the wrong strength or not toxin at all (CDC; FDA).

lessons.title: How fakes were spotted and how to protect yourself
body: The FDA listed the signs of the 2024 counterfeit cartons and vials:

items: Lot number C3709C3 on the carton and vial.
The active ingredient printed as Botulinum Toxin Type A instead of onabotulinumtoxinA.
A 150 unit size, which the maker does not produce.
Text on the carton that is not in English.

body: Those details are specific to one batch, so a new fake may look different. The broader protections are about the setting and the source. The CDC advises using only a licensed provider trained in toxin injection, confirming the product comes from a licensed, FDA-approved source, and watching the dose drawn from a labeled vial (CDC DIY guidance).

Prices far below what other clinics charge, treatments at parties or in homes, and providers who will not show the vial are all warning signs (AAD; AmSpa). Dermatologists reduce the risk by buying directly from the manufacturer, the AAD notes.
If you suspect counterfeit product, report it to the FDA at 800-551-3989 or through its criminal activity reporting form, and report any reaction to MedWatch (FDA).

lessons.title: Contraindications and conditions
body: The labels list two contraindications for every cosmetic toxin: known allergy to any botulinum toxin product or an ingredient, and infection at the planned injection site. Dysport adds known allergy to cow's milk protein, because it may contain trace amounts.

Several conditions call for extra caution and a physician's judgment. People with neuromuscular disorders such as myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome or ALS may be at higher risk of serious weakness, swallowing and breathing problems (Botox Cosmetic label, section 5.6). Existing swallowing or breathing difficulty also raises risk (section 5.7).

The Botox Cosmetic label also advises caution when there is inflammation at the site, an existing droopy eyelid, or a target muscle that is already very weak or wasted, and when a person has heart disease, because cardiovascular events have been reported.
Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, are rare but have been reported, which is one reason toxin belongs in a medical setting with staff who can respond.

Some labels and patient guides add other considerations. Products containing albumin carry a remote theoretical risk related to blood products, and the American Family Physician review lists keloidal scarring among contraindications. Bring your full history to the consultation.

lessons.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and medicines
body: The Botox Cosmetic label says there are no adequate studies in pregnant women. In animal studies, high doses during pregnancy reduced fetal weight and bone development alongside maternal toxicity. For breastfeeding, there are no data on whether the toxin passes into milk (Botox Cosmetic label, sections 8.1 and 8.2).

The largest human dataset is a 29-year review of the manufacturer's safety database. Among 152 live births after exposure, mostly before conception or in the first trimester and mostly at doses under 200 units, the rate of major birth defects was 0.7 percent, consistent with background rates of 3 to 6 percent. The authors note reporting bias and limited data for later pregnancy, and the study was sponsor-run (Brin et al., 2023).

Because cosmetic treatment is elective, most clinicians and patient guides, including Cleveland Clinic, advise waiting until after pregnancy and breastfeeding. If you were treated before you knew you were pregnant, tell your obstetric provider; the data above are reassuring but limited.

Medicines can interact. The labels warn that aminoglycoside antibiotics, curare-like drugs and other agents that interfere with nerve-muscle signaling, as well as muscle relaxants, can strengthen toxin effects. Anticholinergic drugs taken afterward may increase anticholinergic side effects. Toxin from another product or another indication adds to the total (Botox Cosmetic label, section 7).

items: Tell your injector about any antibiotic you are taking or recently finished.
List muscle relaxants, bladder or allergy medicines with anticholinergic effects, and any other toxin treatment, including migraine or sweating treatment.
Mention blood thinners and supplements that raise bruising risk, but do not stop a prescribed medicine without the prescriber's advice.
